artifacts.title: Canberra clergy — newspaper cutting
artifacts.transcription: The printed caption names Rev. D. J. Griffin, Rt. Rev. Dr. Barry, Most Rev. Dr. B. Cattaneo, Rev. P. M. Haydon and Rev. T. M. Dunleavy, from left to right.
artifacts.context: The handwritten heading attributes the cutting to The Canberra Times, 21 February 1928. The printed caption says the group was photographed at the blessing of Canberra on May 8 the previous year. These details are read from the page and await independent source checking.

artifacts.title: Canon F. G. Ward
artifacts.transcription: Canon F. G. Ward / Church of England / Rector in Canberra
artifacts.context: Identification comes from the handwritten caption, not facial recognition. The face detector’s possible-person region remains for human verification.

artifacts.title: A memorial site in Brussels
artifacts.transcription: The stone marks the spot where Nurse Edith Cavell was shot at Brussels.
artifacts.context: The compiler associates this scene with Edith Cavell. The people visible in the photograph are unidentified. Cavell is mentioned by the caption; she is not asserted to be pictured.

artifacts.context: The compiler associates this scene with Edith Cavell. The people visible in the photograph are unidentified. Cavell is mentioned by the caption; she is not asserted to be pictured.

the hospital report which provides for

pital auxiliary, and a hospital commun-
ity chest to be controlled by trustees.

AUSTRALIAN SHIPBUILDING BOARD
SYDNEY
15th August, 1957-
Dear
Chails.
I have received your letter of
August 12 regarding the drawing of the passenger-car
ferry.
It was arranged that a copy of
this should be sent to you, but the young draughtsman
who prepared it decided that he would improve it, and
he is now making a number of minor alterations.
soon as he has completed his work I will have a coloured
print made.
Perhaps you would allow me to have
it suitably framed and engraved, for we would all like
you to accept it from the Australian Shipbuilding Board
as an appreciation of your interest from the early stages
in the building of this vessel.
With kind regards,
Tours sincerely,
Bet hamat
C. H. Maladyen, Esq., C.B.E.,
Secretary,
Department of Shipping and Transport,
497, Collins Street,
MELBOURNE. C.1. VIC.

My dear Senatar,
No message is more welcome to me than
your telegram of today.
Since I had the
pleasure of knowing you first I have recognised
the splendid qualities that are inherent in
you•
It is doubly pleasing to me,
therefore,
to have you acknowledge my service
in such
kind terms.

years is what I have been bound to do in my
service to our country.
It has remained for
you to produce results by a kindly understanding
and a tenacity of purpose which may I say augurs
well for your future career as a Statesman.
May nothing occur which may deter you from
reaching the high places in our political life
which I feel you are destined to achieve.
With best wishes,
Yours very sincerely,
Senator the Hon. Shane Paltridge,

FOR ENGLAND
The bugles of England were blowing
o'er the sea,
As they had called a thousand years,
calling now to me;
They woke me from the dreaming in the
dawning of the day,
The bugles of England
- and how could
I stay!
The banners of England, unfurled across
the sea,
Floating out upon the wind, were
beckoning to me
Storm-rent, and battle-torn, smoke-stained
and grey,
The banners of England - and how could
I stay!
O England! I heard the cry
of those
that died for thee,
Sounding like an organ voice across
the winter sea;
They lived and died for England, and
gladly went their
way.
England!
O England! how could I stay!
J.D. Burns

Dear Mac
You will probably consider this a most shabby
way to treat yo
you after your resuscitating letter of 16/9/30 whose warm
breath fanned to
a bright flame the smouldering embers of my affection, which I could
never
régard as likely to be extinguished; but I have brought this machine home
and the moths are nesting in the ribon and the rust id attacking
its
vitals so that it tends tocreak at the turn of every line, or skid at the
approach thereto; while over all the dust is settling in a feathery
veil to remind me, when I do use it,that I have it only for that space
of time before the dust settles over me and those I wish to write to.
I look to your understanding
of me
to forgive the wrong. As I regard it,
it is a wrong to type a letter, unless it be couched in
the cold lustreles
terms of commerce that have been constructed to match its cold austerity.
I abhor receiving a type written friendly letter, if ther is such a thing!
no matter how comfortably couched, how well composed,how neatly spaced.
To my mind it is like hearing beautiful words from the lips of one whose
face is concealed.
Our handwriting however illegible, carries our person-
ality and representsa personal translation of our
thoughts to paper, as th
though to prove to the reader thatthe writer must have thought the
words to have penned them.
there is a presence, an atmosphere,
Nell known scrall that warms one like the smile on a well-loved face,
howver homely it may be;
but this pretty mask conceals the emotions,

Always the same, polite, efficient, hypocritical it seems to smirk
Our

feel as

well, and it shows you up in a nice

people.name: Charles Hector McFadyen
people.context: Charles Hector McFadyen (1892–1965) served in the First World War and later led the Commonwealth Department of Shipping and Transport. The family identifies him as the compiler of these scrapbooks. Wikipedia cites two volumes held by the McFadyen family; that citation is corroborating context, not an independent authentication of every artifact.

people.name: P. M. Haydon
people.context: The printed caption on Book 1, scan 010 names Rev. P. M. Haydon as the new Canberra parish priest. The handwritten annotation recalls his standing in Queanbeyan and Canberra. This is context from the scrapbook; the identification has not been checked against an external authority.

people.name: T. M. Dunleavy
people.context: The printed caption on Book 1, scan 010 names Rev. T. M. Dunleavy, assistant pastor at Queanbeyan. A handwritten note connects him with boxer Jack Dunleavy. That relationship is the compiler’s assertion and awaits independent confirmation.

people.name: Edith Cavell
people.context: A handwritten caption on Book 1, scan 010 describes a stone marking the place in Brussels where nurse Edith Cavell was shot. The caption supplies the association; this website has not independently verified the location of the photograph.

people.name: F. G. Ward
people.context: The handwritten portrait caption on Book 1, scan 010 identifies Canon F. G. Ward as a Church of England rector in Canberra and a chaplain to the Eighth Brigade, First AIF. This is a transcription of the scrapbook’s attribution, pending external verification.
